title: How do we change centimetres into metres?
description: Lengths in centimetres are written in metres by moving the point two places left, and two lengths are changed back. The video also counts the millimetres in a metre. Keeko's doubt is that four centimetres is zero point four metres.
teaching_notes: One idea: a centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, so the point moves two places. Watch for students who forget the zero that holds the tenths place.

source: Fill in the blanks (cm to m): 36 cm, 50 cm, the cm that make 0.89 m, 4 cm, 325 cm, and the cm that make 2.07 m. How many mm make 1 m, and can we write 1 mm = 1/1000 m?
video_script.why: The child has changed millimetres into centimetres and now changes centimetres into metres.
video_script.substitution: One centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, so the point moves two places when the unit changes.
video_script.anchor: a metre scale cut into one hundred centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: drops the zero that holds the empty tenths place
video_script.payoff_line: Centimetres to metres moves the point two places left

final_answer.spoken: zero point three six, zero point five, zero point eight nine, zero point zero four, three point two five and two point zero seven metres; one thousand millimetres make a metre; yes

video_script.fraction_reading: hundredths and thousandths are said as words
maths_rules: 1 m = 100 cm and 1 cm = 10 mm, so 100 x 10 = 1000 mm
the slip: 0.4 m is 40 cm, not 4 cm
video_script.design: The metre scale stays on the stage with its hundred centimetres; each length slides to its place in the working band and the point moves two places. Keeko's doubt puts the four in the tenths place.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book, then a metre scale cut into 100 cm; lengths 36 cm, 50 cm, 4 cm, 325 cm, 0.89 m and 2.07 m; a question mark in the anchor band

marks.list: the lengths are written beside the scale

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about changing centimetres into metres.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Lengths like thirty-six centimetres, fifty centimetres and four centimetres are to be written in metres.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We also ask how many millimetres make one metre.

beats.on_screen: the lengths stay on the board; Keeko sits beside them as the child
narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a metre scale cut into 100 equal centimetres; one centimetre marked as 1/100 m = 0.01 m

marks.scale: the metre scale is cut into one hundred centimetres
marks.hundredth: one centimetre is marked as 0.01 m

narration: <bookmark mark='scale'/>A metre has one hundred centimetres, so one centimetre is one hundredth of a metre.
<bookmark mark='hundredth'/>That is written zero point zero one metre.

beats.on_screen: Given: 36 cm, 50 cm, 4 cm, 325 cm, 0.89 m and 2.07 m
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, thirty-six, fifty, four and three hundred twenty-five centimetres.
Also zero point eight nine metres and two point zero seven metres.

beats.on_screen: To find: each length in the other unit, and the millimetres in one metre
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to change each length to the other unit, and count the millimetres in a metre.

marks.c50: 50 cm is written as 0.50 m and then 0.5 m

narration: <bookmark mark='c36'/>Step one, one centimetre is zero point zero one metre. Thirty-six centimetres is then zero point three six metres.
<bookmark mark='c50'/>Fifty centimetres is zero point five zero metres, which is zero point five metres.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 4 cm = 0.04 m, with a zero in the tenths place; 325 cm = 3.25 m

marks.c4: 4 drops into hundredths and a zero fills tenths, giving 0.04 m

narration: <bookmark mark='c4'/>Step two, four centimetres has no tenths, so a zero holds the tenths place. It is zero point zero four metres.
<bookmark mark='c325'/>Three hundred twenty-five centimetres is three point two five metres.

marks.back: an arrow shows the other way

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step three, go the other way by multiplying by a hundred.
<bookmark mark='m89'/>Zero point eight nine metres is eighty-nine centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m207'/>Two point zero seven metres is two hundred seven centimetres.

marks.mm: 100 cm and 10 mm per cm are written

narration: <bookmark mark='mm'/>Step four, a metre has one hundred centimetres, and each centimetre is ten millimetres.
<bookmark mark='thou'/>One hundred times ten is one thousand, so one thousand millimetres make one metre.
<bookmark mark='yes'/>One millimetre is then one thousandth of a metre. Yes, one millimetre is zero point zero zero one metre.

marks.l1: the first two lengths are marked
marks.l2: the next two lengths are marked
marks.l3: the last two lengths are marked

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Centimetres to metres moves the point two places left.
<bookmark mark='l1'/>Thirty-six centimetres is zero point three six metres, and fifty centimetres is zero point five metres.
<bookmark mark='l2'/>Eighty-nine centimetres is zero point eight nine metres, and four centimetres is zero point zero four metres.
<bookmark mark='l3'/>Three hundred twenty-five centimetres is three point two five metres.
Two hundred seven centimetres is two point zero seven metres.
<bookmark mark='l4'/>One metre is one thousand millimetres, and yes, one millimetre is one thousandth of a metre.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the metre scale
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 4 cm = 0.4 m appears and is struck out; the scale shows 4 of the 100 parts; 0.04 m is written

marks.fix: 0.4 is struck out and 4 of the 100 parts are shaded
marks.zero: a zero is placed in the tenths place

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks four centimetres is zero point four metres, because the four goes straight after the point.

<bookmark mark='fix'/>But one centimetre is a hundredth of a metre, so the four belongs in the hundredths place. <bookmark mark='zero'/>The tenths place needs a zero, and four centimetres is zero point zero four metres.
